newsitem.title: USA: First Hubble spacewalk on hold.
newsitem.headline: First Hubble spacewalk on hold.

text.p: NASA put on hold the first of four spacewalks to service the Hubble Space Telescope on Thursday after one the observatory's solar panels swung around violently and unexpectedly.

The incident occurred at 9:45 p.m. EST (0245 GMT) as astronauts Mark Lee and Steve Smith, clad in bulky spacesuits, prepared to leave the shuttle's airlock on a spacewalk to install two new scientific instruments aboard the telescope.

"We saw something real unusual," Discovery crewman Joe Tanner informed mission control. "The... array slewed from horizontal to vertical and then about half way back to horizontal." The rapid movement of the 40-ft (12 metre) long array occurred in just five seconds, he said.
"That must have been very dramatic," mission control's Jeff Hoffman replied.

Flight controllers at mission control in Houston believed the right hand array was hit by air venting from the airlock compartment which was mounted in the shuttle's cargo bay for the first time on this mission.
The depressurization of the airlock was halted and the two astronauts remained inside.
Mission control informed the crew they were checking the telescope for any damage and were devising a new method of depressurizing the airlock without affecting the telescope's solar panels.
The astronauts reported the delicate solar array appeared to be unharmed by its sudden rotation.
During Thursday's six-hour spacewalk, astronauts Lee and Smith were to have installed in the telescope two improved scientific instruments, each about the size of a large refrigerator.

A $105 million multipurpose infrared camera will allow astronomers to see deeper into the universe than ever before and may discover planets orbiting other stars, while a $125 million improved spectrograph will help in the search for massive black holes devouring stars in the centre of galaxies.

Upgrades planned over the following three days included the installation of a new digital tape recorder, a more accurate guidance sensor for pointing the telescope and various improved electronic boxes.

Earlier on Thursday the shuttle's robot arm had captured the gleaming 12-ton observatory at 3:33 a.m. EST (0833 GMT) as the two craft soared 360 miles (575 km) above the Pacific Ocean, south west of Mexico.
